text: I
've finished the research and left the tree in a state you can pick up c

old.

## What I found

**The brief's framing was the first thing to fix.** "50 states" implies
50 analyses; the reality is 3 dedicated biometric statutes, 20 com
prehensive privacy laws treating biometrics as sensitive data, and 29 jurisdictions with no collection statute at all. More importantly: **only Illinois l

ets individuals sue you over the scan itself.** That one fact determines nearly all of your launch risk.

**Five states carry real exposure**
— IL (private right of action, fee-shifting, no injury required), TX (no private su
its but a $1.4B AG settlement against Meta, and the tightest retention rule in the country at 1 year), CO (
threshold removed for biometrics, so you're bound from user #1), WA (the statute arguably doesn't re
ach you, but My Health My Data does and it has a private right of action), and CA (consent is easy; the breach exposure is the bi

ggest number in the analysis).

**Three things I'd flag as the most decision-relevant:**

-
The **2024 BIPA amendment** substantially improved your position, and a lot of circulating adv

ice predates it. Per-scan damages are dead; e-signatures now count.
- **Whether you store a template at all** is worth more than any am
ount of consent copy — match-and-discard deletes the California breach exposure entirely. But it does *not* rem

ove the consent duty, and that's the trap.
- I added **automatic-renewal law**, which wasn't in your brief.
It applies in every state, California's AB 2863 has been live since July 2025, and it's more likely to generate your first legal letter than an

ything biometric — an ARL plaintiff needs only a screenshot. Easy to descope if you disagree.

## What

I left you

11 subtasks, ordered so decisions precede build work, each
with the statute cites and numbers already in the description. Two are mar
ked as blocking decisions (Illinois launch scope; storage architecture). The counsel task is deliberately **five narrow questions** rather than a

general review — the survey is done, don't pay for it twice.

Two honest limits: I did not
resolve Washington's "data generated from a photograph" carve-out or Maryland's "strictly necessary" standard, because those need a
lawyer's judgement rather than more searching — they're the first two questions in the counsel task. And I'm not a lawyer; this

is structured research, not advice.

One thing I'd do this week regardless of the Illinois decision: **read your actual insurance w
ording.** BIPA-specific exclusions are now near-ubiquitous in Tech E&O, so you may have zero coverage for the single risk that car
ries a private right of action. Thirty minutes, and it could flip the launch call.
